modules.title: Installing Zoom and Creating Your Account
modules.content:
## Getting Started: Why Zoom Is the First Tool You’ll Reach For

Imagine you’ve just landed a new client. The contract is signed, the first project kickoff call is scheduled for tomorrow at 10 a.m., and the client lives in a different city. You need a reliable way to share your screen, talk face‑to‑face, and record the discussion—all without spending a fortune on hardware or software. In 2023, **Zoom** reported over 300 million daily meeting participants, making it one of the most widely adopted video‑conferencing platforms for businesses of every size. The good news is that the first step—getting Zoom onto your computer or phone and creating an account—takes only a few minutes.

This chapter walks you through every action you need to take, from downloading the client software on Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS, to setting up a personal Zoom account, verifying your email, and configuring basic profile settings. By the end, you’ll know exactly how to start a meeting, and you’ll be aware of the differences between Zoom’s free and paid plans so you can choose the right option for your business needs.

---

## 1. Downloading the Zoom Client

Zoom offers a **client** (the software you install) for desktop operating systems and a **mobile app** for smartphones and tablets. The client provides the richest feature set, including screen sharing, virtual backgrounds, and meeting recordings. Follow the steps that match your device.

### 1.1 Windows (Windows 10 or later)

1. **Open a web browser** (Edge, Chrome, Firefox, etc.) and navigate to the official download page: https://zoom.us/download  
   - *Never download Zoom from third‑party sites; they may contain malware.*

2. Under **“Zoom Client for Meetings,”** click **Download**.  
   - The file will be named something like `ZoomInstaller.exe`.

3. When the download finishes, **run the installer**:
   - Double‑click the file.
   - If Windows asks, click **Yes** to allow the program to make changes to your device.

4. The installer will first download the latest version of the client, then launch the **Zoom Setup Wizard**.  
   - Click **Install** and wait for the progress bar to complete.

5. When installation is finished, click **Close**.  
   - The Zoom icon (a blue video camera) will appear on your desktop and in the system tray (bottom‑right corner of the screen).

### 1.2 macOS (macOS 10.10 or later)

1. Open **Safari** (or any other browser) and go to https://zoom.us/download.

2. Click **Download** under **“Zoom Client for Meetings.”**  
   - The file will be named `Zoom.pkg`.

3. Locate the downloaded file in the **Downloads** folder and double‑click it.

4. The macOS installer will open. Click **Continue**, then **Install**.  
   - You may be prompted to enter your **administrator password**; type it and press **Enter**.

5. After the installation completes, click **Close**.  
   - The Zoom app will be added to your **Applications** folder and can be launched from Launchpad or Spotlight.

### 1.3 Android Devices (smartphones and tablets)

1. Open the **Google Play Store**.

2. In the search bar, type **“Zoom Cloud Meetings.”**  
   - Verify that the publisher is **Zoom Video Communications, Inc.** (the official publisher).

3. Tap **Install**.  
   - The app will download and automatically install.

4. Once installed, tap **Open** to launch Zoom.

### 1.4 iOS Devices (iPhone, iPad)

1. Open the **App Store**.

2. Search for **“Zoom Cloud Meetings.”**  
   - Confirm the developer is **Zoom Video Communications, Inc.**

3. Tap the **Get** button, then **Install**.  
   - You may need to authenticate with Face ID, Touch ID, or your Apple ID password.

4. After installation, tap **Open** to start the app.

---

## 2. Creating Your Personal Zoom Account

A **Zoom account** is a unique login that lets you host meetings, schedule events, and personalize your profile. You can create an account with an email address or use a Single Sign‑On (SSO) service like Google or Microsoft. For beginners, the email‑based method is simplest.

### 2.1 Sign‑Up Using an Email Address

1. **Launch the Zoom client** (desktop) or **open the Zoom app** (mobile).  
   - On the welcome screen, click **Sign Up Free**.

2. **Enter your work email address** (or any email you check regularly).  
   - Zoom will send a verification email to this address.  
   - *Tip:* Use a professional email (e.g., yourname@yourcompany.com) to keep your business identity clear.

3. Click **Sign Up**. The next screen asks you to **confirm your age** (Zoom is for users 18 years or older). Choose **Yes** if you meet the requirement.

4. **Check your inbox** for an email titled “Activate your Zoom account.”  
   - If you don’t see it, look in the **Spam/Junk** folder.

5. Open the email and click the **Activate** button.  
   - This redirects you to a page where you set a **password**. Choose a strong password (at least 8 characters, mixing letters, numbers, and symbols).

6. Click **Continue**. You’re now signed in and taken to the **Zoom web portal** (zoom.us/profile).

### 2.2 Sign‑Up Using Google or Microsoft

If you already have a Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 account, you can click the respective **Sign up with Google** or **Sign up with Microsoft** button on the sign‑up page. After you grant Zoom permission to access your basic profile information, you’ll be redirected back to Zoom, where you’ll still need to verify your email (the same process as above).

### 2.3 Verifying Your Email Address

Even if you clicked the activation link, Zoom may still ask you to **verify** the email during your first login:

1. After signing in, a banner may appear: **“Verify your email address.”**  
2. Click **Resend Verification Email** if you didn’t receive the first one.  
3. Follow the same steps—open the email and click **Verify**.

### 2.4 Setting Up Basic Profile Preferences

A well‑filled profile helps meeting participants recognize you and builds trust.

1. From the **Zoom web portal**, click **Profile** on the left navigation bar.

2. **Name** – This is the name displayed in meeting participant lists.  
   - Use your **full name** or the name you prefer for business communication (e.g., “Jane Doe, Project Manager”).

3. **Photo** – Click the **Change** icon (camera) next to the default avatar.  
   - Upload a professional headshot (square image, 200 × 200 px works well).  
   - A clear photo helps attendees feel they’re speaking with a real person.

4. **Time Zone** – Zoom schedules meetings based on your time zone.  
   - Click the dropdown and select your correct **region** (e.g., “Eastern Time (US & Canada)”).  
   - If you travel frequently, you can change this later; Zoom will automatically adjust scheduled meetings.

5. **Personal Meeting ID (PMI)** – By default, Zoom generates a random 10‑digit ID for your personal meeting room.  
   - You can **customize** it to something memorable (e.g., “123‑456‑7890”).  
   - **Do not** share your PMI publicly unless you intend it to be a permanent “open door” meeting space.

6. Click **Save** after making any changes.

---

## 3. Understanding Zoom’s Plan Options

Zoom offers a **Free (Basic) plan** and several **Paid (Pro, Business, Enterprise)** tiers. Knowing the limits of each helps you decide whether the free version suffices for your early business needs or if a paid upgrade is justified.

| Feature | Free (Basic) | Pro | Business | Enterprise |
|---------|--------------|-----|----------|------------|
| **Meeting duration** | 40 minutes per group meeting (2‑person unlimited) | 30 hours | 30 hours | 30 hours |
| **Participants per meeting** | Up to 100 | Up to 100 (can increase) | Up to 300 | Up to 500 |
| **Cloud recording storage** | None (local recording only) | 1 GB | 1 GB per license | Unlimited |
| **Custom personal meeting ID** | Yes (but limited) | Yes, with branding | Yes, with branding | Yes, with branding |
| **Admin controls & reporting** | No | Basic reporting | Advanced reporting, user management | Full enterprise admin console |
| **Support** | Email support (24 h) | 24/7 phone & email | 24/7 phone & email | Dedicated account manager (optional) |

### 3.1 When the Free Plan Is Enough

- **One‑off client calls**: If you only need occasional meetings under 40 minutes, the free plan works well.
- **One‑to‑one consultations**: Unlimited 1‑on‑1 meetings have no time limit.
- **Small‑team brainstorming**: Up to 100 participants is sufficient for many start‑ups.

### 3.2 Signs You Might Need a Paid Plan

- **Recurring weekly meetings** that exceed 40 minutes.
- **Need for cloud recordings** (e.g., for compliance or sharing with absent team members).
- **Branding requirements** such as a custom meeting URL (e.g., `yourcompany.zoom.us`).
- **Advanced admin controls** (e.g., managing multiple users, enforcing security policies).

If you’re unsure, start with the free plan; you can upgrade anytime from the **Billing** section of your Zoom account.

---

## 4. Step‑by‑Step Walkthrough: From Download to First Meeting

Below is a consolidated, numbered checklist that mirrors the flow a new user will experience. Use it as a quick reference or print it out for onboarding new staff.

1. **Download the client** appropriate for your device (Windows, macOS, Android, iOS).  
2. **Install** the software following the on‑screen prompts.  
3. **Launch Zoom** and click **Sign Up Free**.  
4. **Enter your professional email** and confirm you’re 18 or older.  
5. **Check your inbox** for the activation email; click **Activate**.  
6. **Create a strong password** and complete the sign‑up flow.  
7. **Verify your email** (if prompted) by clicking the verification link.  
8. **Open the Zoom web portal** (zoom.us/profile) to edit your **profile**: name, photo, time zone, personal meeting ID.  
9. **Explore the plan options** under **Billing** → **Upgrade** to see what each tier offers.  
10. **Test a meeting**:  
    - Click **New Meeting** in the client.  
    - Click **Invite** → **Copy Invite Link** and paste it into a test email to a colleague.  
    - End the meeting after a few minutes to confirm everything works.

---

## 5. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Even seasoned users sometimes encounter simple mistakes during installation and account creation. Anticipating these issues saves time and frustration.

| Problem | Likely Cause | Solution |
|---------|--------------|----------|
| **Zoom won’t open after installation** | Antivirus or firewall blocking the executable | Add Zoom to the **exception list** of your security software; reinstall if necessary |
| **“Invalid email address” error** | Typo in email or using a disposable address | Re‑enter a valid, permanent email (preferably your corporate address) |
| **No verification email received** | Email filtered as spam or corporate email policy | Check **Spam/Junk** folders; ask IT to whitelist `@zoom.us` domains |
| **Cannot change time zone** | Account is linked to an organization that enforces a fixed zone | Contact your Zoom admin or use a personal (non‑SSO) account |
| **Meeting ends after 40 minutes** | Using the Free plan for a group meeting | Upgrade to a paid plan or schedule a new meeting after the limit expires |

---

## 6. Best Practices for a Business‑Ready Setup

While this chapter focuses on the initial download and account creation, adopting a few best practices now will smooth the transition to more advanced features later.

1. **Use a dedicated business email** for your Zoom account rather than a personal address. This separates work communication and eases future user management.
2. **Enable Two‑Factor Authentication (2FA)** under **Settings → Security** to protect against unauthorized access.
3. **Download the latest client version** regularly; Zoom releases monthly updates that include security patches and new features.
4. **Set a professional profile photo** and ensure your display name matches your corporate branding.
5. **Bookmark the Zoom web portal** (`https://zoom.us/signin`) for quick access to account settings, billing, and meeting history.

---

## 7. Quick Reference: Keyboard Shortcuts (Desktop Only)

Learning a few shortcuts can speed up your workflow once you start hosting meetings.

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| **Alt + A** (Windows) / **Command + Shift + A** (macOS) | Mute/Unmute audio |
| **Alt + V** (Windows) / **Command + Shift + V** (macOS) | Start/Stop video |
| **Alt + S** (Windows) / **Command + Shift + S** (macOS) | Share screen |
| **Alt + Q** (Windows) / **Command + Shift + Q** (macOS) | End meeting |
| **Alt + I** (Windows) / **Command + Shift + I** (macOS) | Open/close chat panel |

---

## 8. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

**Q: Can I use the same Zoom account on multiple devices?**  
A: Yes. Your account syncs across all installations; you can sign in on a laptop, tablet, and phone simultaneously.

**Q: Do I need to install the desktop client to join a meeting?**  
A: No. Participants can join via a web browser, but the client provides the best experience (screen sharing, virtual backgrounds, etc.).

**Q: What if I lose access to my email address?**  
A: Use the **Forgot Password** link on the sign‑in page to reset credentials. If the email is no longer reachable, contact Zoom Support to change the primary email after verifying ownership.

**Q: Is there a limit to how many meetings I can schedule?**  
A: No. The free plan limits the *duration* of group meetings, not the number of scheduled meetings.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Download and install** the Zoom client for your operating system (Windows, macOS, Android, iOS) directly from the official Zoom website or app stores.  
- **Create a personal Zoom account** using a professional email, verify it through the activation link, and set a strong password.  
- **Customize your profile**—name, photo, time zone, and personal meeting ID—to present a consistent business identity.  
- **Understand plan limits**: the Free plan offers unlimited 1‑on‑1 meetings and 40‑minute group sessions, while paid tiers provide longer meeting durations, larger participant caps, cloud recordings, and advanced admin controls.  
- **Avoid common pitfalls** by checking spam folders, whitelisting Zoom domains, and enabling two‑factor authentication.  

With Zoom installed and your account fully configured, you’re ready to move on to the next step: learning how to navigate the Zoom interface and schedule your first business meeting.

modules.title: Understanding the Zoom Interface
modules.content:
## A Day‑to‑Day Example: Maya’s First Business Call  

Maya has just finished the steps in **Chapter 1**—she downloaded the Zoom client, ran the installer, and created her Zoom account. The next time she opens the Zoom client, she sees a new screen filled with icons, menus, and options. She needs to know where to click to start a meeting with a client, how to make sure her camera and microphone are ready, and where to find help if something looks unfamiliar. The walkthrough below shows exactly what Maya (and anyone new to Zoom for business) should look for the first time they log in.

---

## 1. The Main Dashboard: Home, Meetings, Contacts, Settings  

When Maya launches the **Zoom Client for Meetings**, the first window that appears is the **Home** tab. This tab is the central hub; everything else branches out from here.

| Tab | Icon (desktop) | What You’ll Find | Typical Use |
|-----|----------------|------------------|-------------|
| **Home** | House | Quick‑start “New Meeting,” “Join,” recent meetings, personal meeting ID | Jump straight into a call or join one you’ve been invited to |
| **Meetings** | Calendar | Scheduled meetings, past meetings, personal meeting ID, recurring meetings | Organize, edit, or start meetings you’ve already set up |
| **Contacts** | People | Your Zoom contacts, invitation options, status (online/offline) | Connect with colleagues or external partners |
| **Settings** | Gear | Audio, video, virtual background, advanced options, help resources | Customize how Zoom works for you |

> **Tip:** The tabs run across the top of the client on a desktop, or appear as a bottom navigation bar on the mobile app. Clicking any tab instantly swaps the main pane without opening a new window.

### 1.1 Home Tab – Your Launch Pad  

- **New Meeting** – Starts an instant meeting using your default audio/video settings.  
- **Join** – Lets you enter a meeting by typing a Meeting ID or personal link.  
- **Personal Meeting ID (PMI)** – A permanent 10‑digit number (or link) that belongs to your account. It appears right under the “Join” button; you can copy it for quick sharing.  
- **Recent** – Shows the last few meetings you attended, letting you re‑join or view recordings.

### 1.2 Meetings Tab – Scheduling Hub  

Even though scheduling is covered later, the **Meetings** tab is where Maya will eventually see a list of all her upcoming appointments. For now, she can:

- **Personal Link Settings** – Click the *Personal Link* row to edit the URL that points to her PMI (e.g., `https://zoom.us/j/1234567890`).  
- **Recurring Meeting** – Set up a meeting that repeats (daily, weekly, etc.)—useful for weekly team stand‑ups.

### 1.3 Contacts Tab – Building Your Network  

- **Add Contact** – Invite someone by email; they receive an invitation to join Zoom if they don’t already have an account.  
- **Status Icons** – Green circle = online, gray = offline, red = busy. Knowing a contact’s status helps Maya decide when to call.

### 1.4 Settings Tab – Personalizing Zoom  

All the “default” preferences Maya will use for every meeting live here. The Settings tab is divided into sections that we’ll explore in the next part of this chapter.

---

## 2. Personal Meeting ID and Personal Link Settings  

The **Personal Meeting ID (PMI)** is a convenient shortcut for recurring one‑to‑one or small‑group calls. Maya can share her PMI or the associated **Personal Link** with clients so they never have to type a long numeric ID.

### 2.1 Finding Your PMI  

1. Click the **Meetings** tab.  
2. The top of the pane shows **Personal Meeting ID** and the numeric code.  
3. Directly below, the **Personal Link** appears as a clickable URL.

### 2.2 Editing the Personal Link  

- Click the **Edit** (pencil) icon next to the link.  
- Change the suffix (the part after `/j/`) to something memorable, e.g., `johnsmith`. The new link becomes `https://zoom.us/j/johnsmith`.  
- **Save** the change. The link now redirects to Maya’s PMI while keeping the numeric ID intact.

> **Why it matters:** A readable link reduces typing errors and looks more professional when shared in email signatures or calendar invites.

### 2.3 Security Tip for PMI  

If Maya wants extra protection, she can require a **meeting password** for her PMI. This option appears under **Personal Meeting ID** → **Require meeting password**. She can set a simple password (e.g., `Biz2024`) and share it only with trusted participants.

---

## 3. Configuring Default Audio, Video, and Virtual Backgrounds  

Before Maya’s first client call, she should decide what Zoom should automatically enable when she starts a meeting. These preferences live in the **Settings** tab.

### 3.1 Audio Settings  

1. Open **Settings** → **Audio**.  
2. **Microphone** – Choose the device (built‑in laptop mic, USB headset, etc.).  
3. **Speaker** – Select where you want to hear others (laptop speakers, headphones).  
4. **Test Speaker** / **Test Mic** – Click to verify sound levels.  
5. **Automatically join audio by computer when joining a meeting** – Turn **ON** to skip the “Join Audio” prompt.  
6. **Suppress background noise** – Choose *Low*, *Medium*, or *High* based on your environment.

> **Pro tip:** If Maya uses a headset, enabling “Automatically join audio” prevents the echo that sometimes occurs with built‑in speakers and microphones.

### 3.2 Video Settings  

1. In **Settings**, select **Video**.  
2. **Camera** – Pick the webcam you want to use (built‑in, external USB, or a virtual camera).  
3. **Enable HD** – Turns on high‑definition video if your internet bandwidth allows it.  
4. **Touch up my appearance** – A light skin‑smoothing filter; useful for a polished look.  
5. **Mirror my video** – Shows a mirrored preview; keep it **OFF** if you want the video to appear as others see it.

### 3.3 Virtual Backgrounds  

Virtual backgrounds let Maya replace her real background with an image or video, handy when her home office is cluttered.

1. Click **Background & Filters** (still within Settings).  
2. **Choose a default background** – Zoom ships with a few professional images (e.g., a simple gradient or office setting).  
3. **Add Image** – Click the **+** icon to upload a company logo or branded backdrop.  
4. **Video Filter** – Optional moving backgrounds for a more dynamic feel.  

> **Note:** Using a virtual background without a green screen works best when the webcam can clearly separate you from your surroundings. If Maya experiences a blurry edge, she can enable the **“I have a green screen”** option and upload a green‑screen image.

### 3.4 Saving Your Choices  

All changes are saved automatically. The next time Maya clicks **New Meeting**, Zoom will launch with the microphone, camera, and virtual background she selected.

---

## 4. Quick Access to Help Resources and Account Management  

Even the most prepared user may run into an unexpected issue. Zoom embeds several help and account tools directly in the client.

### 4.1 Help Center  

- Click the **?** (question‑mark) icon in the upper‑right corner of the client.  
- Options appear: **Help Center**, **Keyboard Shortcuts**, **Video Settings**, **Audio Settings**, and **Contact Support**.  
- Selecting **Help Center** opens a web page with searchable articles, tutorials, and community forums.

### 4.2 Account Management  

Within the **Settings** tab, scroll to the bottom and click **Profile**.

- **Edit My Profile** – Opens a browser window to the Zoom web portal where Maya can change her name, profile picture, and time zone.  
- **Sign Out** – Logs her out of the client; useful if she shares a workstation.  
- **Upgrade Account** – Directs to a page where she can purchase a Business or Enterprise plan if her organization needs additional features (e.g., larger meeting capacity).

### 4.3 In‑Client Feedback  

If Maya encounters a bug, she can click **?** → **Send Feedback**. This sends a report to Zoom’s support team, optionally attaching a screenshot.

### 4.4 Keyboard Shortcuts (Bonus)  

A quick way to navigate without mouse clicks:

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| `Alt + H` (Windows) / `⌘ + Shift + H` (Mac) | Open **Home** tab |
| `Alt + M` / `⌘ + Shift + M` | Open **Meetings** tab |
| `Alt + A` / `⌘ + Shift + A` | Toggle **Audio** mute/unmute |
| `Alt + V` / `⌘ + Shift + V` | Toggle **Video** on/off |

Maya can view the full list by selecting **Keyboard Shortcuts** from the **?** menu.

---

## 5. Putting It All Together: A Mini‑Walkthrough  

1. **Launch the Zoom client** – Maya sees the **Home** tab.  
2. **Check audio/video** – She clicks **Settings → Audio** and **Settings → Video** to confirm her headset and webcam are selected.  
3. **Set a virtual background** – In **Settings → Background & Filters**, she uploads her company logo.  
4. **Copy her Personal Link** – She goes to **Meetings**, taps the **Edit** icon next to the link, and copies `https://zoom.us/j/johnsmith`.  
5. **Invite a client** – Maya pastes the link into an email, adds the meeting password, and clicks **Send**.  
6. **Start the call** – When the client joins, Maya clicks **Home → New Meeting**; the meeting launches with her pre‑selected audio, video, and background already active.  
7. **If something goes wrong** – She clicks the **?** icon, selects **Help Center**, and follows the guided steps.

Through this simple sequence, Maya has used every interface element covered in this chapter, turning a potentially confusing screen into a predictable workflow.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **Home**, **Meetings**, **Contacts**, and **Settings** tabs are the four pillars of the Zoom client’s interface.  
- Your **Personal Meeting ID** and **Personal Link** provide a permanent, easy way to host recurring calls; they can be edited for readability and secured with a password.  
- Default **audio**, **video**, and **virtual background** settings live in the **Settings** tab and apply automatically to every new meeting you start.  
- The **?** icon gives instant access to the Help Center, keyboard shortcuts, and feedback tools, while the **Profile** section under Settings handles account‑level changes.  
- By confirming preferences before the first call, you ensure a smooth, professional experience for both you and your business contacts.

modules.title: Scheduling and Managing Meetings
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Situation: The Weekly Team Sync

Imagine you’re the project coordinator for a small marketing agency. Every Monday at 9 a.m. EST you need to bring together three copywriters, two designers, and a client‑service lead for a 30‑minute status update. The team is spread across New York, London, and Sydney, so you must make sure the meeting appears correctly on each participant’s calendar, is protected by a password, and can be started with a single click.  

All of this can be set up **before the first meeting even begins**—using only the Zoom desktop client or the Zoom web portal. The steps below walk you through exactly how to do that, from a one‑time call to a recurring series, adding participants, tweaking security, and keeping everything tidy.

---

## Scheduling a One‑Time Meeting with the Desktop Client

The Zoom desktop client (the “Zoom Client for Meetings” you installed in *Chapter 1*) is the quickest way to create a single meeting.

1. **Open the Zoom Client** and sign in if you aren’t already.  
   > *Tip:* If you see the “Start” button instead of “Sign In,” you’re already logged in.

2. **Click the “Schedule” icon** (calendar with a plus sign) on the home screen.  
   This opens the **Schedule Meeting** window.

3. **Enter the meeting basics**  

   | Field | What to enter | Why it matters |
   |-------|---------------|----------------|
   | **Topic** | *Weekly Team Sync – Marketing* | Appears as the meeting title in invites and calendars. |
   | **When** | Choose the date and start time. | Zoom automatically converts the time to each participant’s local zone. |
   | **Duration** | 30 minutes (or “No Fixed Time”) | Helps participants block the right amount of time on their calendars. |
   | **Time Zone** | *Eastern Time (US & Canada)* – or let Zoom detect your system’s zone. | Critical when you have attendees in multiple regions. |
   | **Meeting ID** | *Generate Automatically* (default) | Keeps the ID unique and hard to guess. |
   | **Password** | *Enter a 6‑digit password* (e.g., 842931) | Adds a layer of security; required for most business accounts. |

4. **Select the video and audio defaults**  

   - *Host video:* On (or Off if you prefer to start muted).  
   - *Participant video:* Off (common for status‑update calls).  
   - *Audio:* “Both” (allows participants to join by phone or computer).

5. **Enable meeting options** (more detail in the “Meeting Options” section below). For a one‑time call you may simply tick **“Enable waiting room”**.

6. **Save the meeting** by clicking **“Save.”**  

   - Zoom will automatically open the meeting’s details page.  
   - From here you can copy the invitation, add it to a calendar, or edit later.

### Adding Participants Directly from the Desktop Client

On the meeting details page, look for the **“Invite”** button.

- **Email invitation:** Click **“Copy Invitation”**, paste into your email client, and add recipients.  
- **Meeting link:** The invitation includes a URL (e.g., `https://zoom.us/j/1234567890?pwd=abcd`). Sending just the link works for participants who already have the Zoom client installed.

---

## Scheduling a Recurring Meeting

A *recurring meeting* is a series that repeats on a set schedule (daily, weekly, monthly, etc.). This is perfect for your Monday sync.

1. Follow steps 1‑3 above, then **check the box “Recurrence.”**  

2. **Choose the recurrence pattern**  

   - **Frequency:** Weekly  
   - **Repeat every:** 1 week  
   - **Day:** Monday  
   - **End date:** Either “No end date” or pick a specific date (e.g., 30 June 2026).

3. **Set the same meeting options** (password, waiting room, etc.) as you would for a one‑time meeting.

4. **Save** the series. Zoom creates a single meeting entry that represents the whole series, making it easy to edit all occurrences at once.

> **Pro tip:** If you need a slightly different agenda for a particular week, you can edit that single occurrence later without affecting the rest of the series.

---

## Scheduling from the Zoom Web Portal

Sometimes you may prefer a browser—especially when you’re on a computer without the desktop client installed.

1. **Open a web browser** (Safari, Chrome, Edge, etc.) and go to `https://zoom.us/signin`.  
   Sign in with the same credentials you used for the desktop client.

2. In the left‑hand navigation menu, click **“Meetings.”**  

3. Click the **“Schedule a New Meeting”** button at the top right.

4. The web form mirrors the desktop client’s fields: **Topic, When, Duration, Time Zone, Meeting ID, Password, Video, Audio, and Recurrence**. Fill them in just as described earlier.

5. **Calendar integration options** appear at the bottom of the page (Google Calendar, Outlook Calendar, iCal). Choose the one you use; Zoom will generate a ready‑to‑send invitation.

6. Click **“Save.”** The meeting now appears in your **“Upcoming Meetings”** list on the portal, where you can edit, copy, or delete it later.

> **Why use the web portal?**  
> - It works on any device with a browser, even if you can’t install the client.  
> - It provides a quick overview of *all* scheduled meetings in one place, which is handy for administrators managing multiple accounts.

---

## Adding Participants: Three Simple Ways

### 1. Email Invitation (the classic)

- From the **meeting details page** (desktop or web), click **“Copy Invitation.”**  
- Paste into your email client (Outlook, Gmail, etc.).  
- The invitation includes: meeting link, meeting ID, password, dial‑in numbers (if enabled), and a “Add to Calendar” button.

### 2. Calendar Integration

When you schedule a meeting, Zoom can automatically create a calendar event:

| Calendar | How it works |
|----------|--------------|
| **Google Calendar** | After saving, click **“Add to Google Calendar.”** A new event opens with the Zoom link pre‑filled. Invite participants by adding their email addresses in the “Guests” field. |
| **Outlook Calendar** | Click **“Outlook Calendar.”** A `.ics` file downloads; open it in Outlook, then add attendees. |
| **iCal (Apple Calendar)** | Click **“iCal.”** The file adds the event to your Mac’s Calendar app, where you can invite others. |

The calendar entry syncs any changes you make later (e.g., new password) back to the participants’ calendars.

### 3. Direct Meeting Link

If you prefer a lightweight approach, simply send the URL (`https://zoom.us/j/…`) via instant messaging, Slack, or a project‑management tool. Participants click the link and are prompted to launch the Zoom client or join via their browser.

> **Security reminder:** Even when sharing a link, keep the meeting password private and change it periodically for recurring meetings.

---

## Meeting Options and Security Settings

Zoom provides a toolbox of options that control what happens before and during a meeting. All of them are accessible from the **“Meeting Options”** section when you schedule, and many can be toggled on/off later.

| Option | Description | Typical Use |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| **Password** | A numeric or alphanumeric code required to join. | Prevents “Zoombombing.” |
| **Waiting Room** | Participants wait in a virtual lobby until the host admits them. | Gives the host control over who enters, especially useful for large or public meetings. |
| **Enable Join Before Host** | Allows participants to enter the meeting before the host arrives. | Handy for webinars where attendees need to settle early. |
| **Mute Participants Upon Entry** | Automatically silences everyone when they join. | Reduces background noise in large calls. |
| **Allow Participants to Rename Themselves** | Lets attendees change their displayed name. | Turn off for corporate meetings to maintain identity consistency. |
| **Record Automatically** | Starts recording as soon as the meeting begins. | Useful for training sessions; note that recordings are stored according to your account’s settings. |
| **Breakout Room Pre‑Assign** | (Covered later) – you can pre‑define breakout rooms now. | Not needed for a simple sync. |

### Configuring the Waiting Room

1. In the **Meeting Options** area, tick **“Enable waiting room.”**  
2. Click **“Edit”** next to the waiting room label to customize the message participants see (e.g., “Please wait while the host starts the meeting.”).  

When participants click the meeting link, they’ll see this message until you admit them from the **“Participants”** pane during the live meeting.

### Host Controls

- **Host Key:** A 6‑digit PIN that lets you claim host rights if you lose them (e.g., after joining from a different device). Set it in **Settings → Meeting → Host Key** on the web portal.  
- **Co‑Host:** Assign another participant the ability to manage participants, start recordings, or share screens. This can be set during the meeting or pre‑assigned via the **“Alternative Hosts”** field when scheduling.

---

## Editing, Copying, and Deleting Scheduled Meetings

Even the best‑planned meetings sometimes need tweaks. Zoom lets you manage scheduled sessions from both the desktop client and the web portal.

### Editing a Meeting

1. Locate the meeting in **“Upcoming Meetings”** (desktop: Home → “Meetings” tab; web: Meetings → Upcoming).  
2. Click the meeting name, then click **“Edit.”**  
3. Change any field—time, password, participants, etc.  
4. Click **“Save.”**  
   - If the meeting is already in participants’ calendars, Zoom will send an update notification automatically.

### Copying a Meeting

When you need a new meeting that shares most settings with an existing one (e.g., a similar training session):

1. In the **Upcoming Meetings** list, hover over the meeting and click the **“Copy”** icon (two overlapping squares).  
2. A new meeting form appears with all fields pre‑filled. Adjust the **Topic**, **Date**, or **Recurrence** as needed, then **Save**.

### Deleting a Meeting

1. Find the meeting you wish to remove.  
2. Click the **“Delete”** button (trash can icon).  
3. Confirm the deletion.  

> **Note:** Deleting a meeting removes it from your Zoom account and cancels any pending calendar invitations. Participants will receive a cancellation notice.

---

## Understanding Time‑Zone Handling

Zoom stores all meeting times in **Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)** on its servers. When you schedule a meeting, the client or portal converts your local time to UTC, then displays the time back in the viewer’s local zone.

- **Why it matters:** If you schedule a meeting at 9 a.m. EST and travel to London, the meeting will still start at 9 a.m. EST for attendees—Zoom will automatically show you the correct local time (2 p.m. GMT).  
- **Changing the time zone:** In the **Schedule Meeting** window, click the **Time Zone** dropdown and select a different zone. Zoom will recalculate the UTC value, keeping the displayed local time consistent for you.

### Dealing with Daylight‑Saving Time (DST)

Zoom automatically adjusts for DST changes based on the selected time zone. However, if you schedule a recurring meeting far into the future, double‑check the meeting time after DST transitions to ensure it still aligns with your intended local hour.

---

## Calendar Integration: Keeping Everything in Sync

Most business users rely on a calendar app to see upcoming commitments. Zoom’s integration makes sure your meetings appear where you already look.

1. **During scheduling**, select the appropriate calendar option (Google, Outlook, iCal).  
2. Zoom generates a calendar event that includes:  

   - **Title** (the meeting topic)  
   - **Date & time** (converted to the calendar’s time zone)  
   - **Zoom link** and **password**  
   - **Dial‑in numbers** (if enabled)  

3. **Invite participants** directly from the calendar interface.  

4. **When you edit the meeting**, Zoom pushes the changes to the calendar event, and attendees receive an update automatically.

> **Tip for beginners:** If you’re not sure which calendar you use, start with Google Calendar—it’s free, web‑based, and works on Android, iOS, and desktop browsers.

---

## Quick Reference Checklist

- **One‑time vs. recurring:** Choose “Recurrence” for weekly/monthly series.  
- **Add participants:** Email copy, calendar invite, or plain link.  
- **Secure the meeting:** Set a password, enable waiting room, consider mute‑on‑entry.  
- **Edit later:** Use the “Edit” button; changes sync to calendars.  
- **Copy for similar meetings:** Click the copy icon to duplicate settings.  
- **Time zones:** Verify the zone before saving; Zoom handles DST automatically.  
- **Calendar sync:** Pick your calendar type; Zoom will keep events up‑to‑date.

---

## ## Key Takeaways

- **Scheduling** can be done from either the Zoom desktop client or the web portal; both present the same core fields.  
- **Recurring meetings** are created by ticking “Recurrence” and defining the pattern (weekly, monthly, etc.).  
- **Participants** can be invited via email copy, calendar integration (Google, Outlook, iCal), or a simple meeting link.  
- **Meeting options**—password, waiting room, mute‑on‑entry, and host controls—provide essential security and flow management.  
- **Editing, copying, and deleting** meetings are straightforward actions available from the “Upcoming Meetings” list; changes automatically update calendar invites.  
- **Zoom stores times in UTC**, so selecting the correct time zone ensures all attendees see the right local time, even across daylight‑saving changes.  
- **Calendar integration** keeps your Zoom meetings visible alongside other commitments, and any schedule changes propagate automatically.

With these tools, you can confidently set up any business call—whether it’s a one‑off client demo or a weekly internal sync—while keeping participants informed, secure, and on time.

modules.title: Running a Live Meeting
modules.content:
## Jump‑in Example: The 15‑Minute Pitch  

Imagine you’re about to present a new product to a potential client. The meeting is scheduled for 10 a.m., and you’ve just opened the **Zoom Client for Meetings** on your laptop. The client has joined from a web browser, while a colleague will dial in from a smartphone. You have only a few minutes to make sure everyone can see and hear you, that the conversation stays focused, and that you can share a slide deck without any hiccups.  

The following sections walk you through exactly what you need to do—starting the meeting, keeping the audio‑visual flow smooth, engaging participants, and sharing content—so you can deliver that pitch confidently.

---

## 1. Starting a Meeting from Any Device  

Zoom lets you launch a meeting from three main entry points: the **client** (desktop app), a **web browser**, or the **mobile app**. All three follow the same underlying process, but the interface differs slightly.

### 1.1 From the Zoom Client (Desktop)  

1. **Open the client** – double‑click the “Zoom Client for Meetings” icon you installed earlier.  
2. **Sign in** – use the credentials you created when you *Installed Zoom and Created Your Account*.  
3. **Locate the meeting** –  
   * If you scheduled it in **Scheduling and Managing Meetings**, it will appear under the **Meetings** tab.  
   * Click the meeting’s name, then click **Start**.  
4. The meeting window opens. You’ll see your own video (if your camera is on) and a toolbar at the bottom.

### 1.2 From a Web Browser  

1. **Open a browser** – Safari, Chrome, Edge, or Firefox will work.  
2. **Navigate to** `https://zoom.us/join`.  
3. **Enter the Meeting ID** that you received in the invitation email.  
4. **Click Join** – you’ll be prompted to download a small “Zoom Web Client” plug‑in if you haven’t used the web version before; accept it.  
5. Choose **Join from Browser** when the option appears.  
6. After a brief loading screen, you’re in the meeting.

### 1.3 From the Mobile App  

1. **Launch “Zoom Cloud Meetings”** (the app you downloaded from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store).  
2. **Tap Join** and type the Meeting ID, or tap the meeting link directly from your email or calendar.  
3. **Allow permissions** for microphone and camera when the system asks.  
4. **Tap Join** again to enter the room.

> **Tip:** No matter which device you use, the first screen you see is the *pre‑join* screen where you can test your microphone and camera. Take a moment to confirm that you can see yourself and hear your voice clearly before you click **Join** or **Start**.

---

## 2. Managing Audio and Video Settings  

Once the meeting is live, keeping the audio‑video environment orderly is essential. Zoom provides quick controls on the toolbar and deeper settings in the **Audio** and **Video** panels.

### 2.1 Quick Toolbar Controls  

| Icon | Action |
|------|--------|
| **Microphone** (red line) | Click to **mute/unmute** yourself. |
| **Camera** (camera icon) | Click to **stop/start video**. |
| **Speaker** (headphone) | Opens **Audio Settings** for device selection and volume. |
| **Video Settings** (gear) | Opens **Video Settings** for camera choice, aspect ratio, and virtual background. |

> **Pro tip:** For a professional presentation, keep your microphone **muted** when you’re not speaking to avoid background noise.

### 2.2 Host‑Only Controls  

As the meeting host (the user who started the meeting or was assigned host rights), you can manage participants’ audio and video:

1. **Mute All Participants** – Click the **Participants** button, then **Mute All** at the bottom of the panel.  
2. **Allow Unmute** – After muting everyone, you can optionally let participants unmute themselves by checking **Allow participants to unmute themselves**.  
3. **Spotlight Video** – To draw attention to a specific speaker (e.g., the client presenting), hover over their name in the Participants list, click **More**, then select **Spotlight Video**. This pins their video for everyone, overriding gallery view.

### 2.3 Advanced Audio Options  

- **Suppress Background Noise** – In **Audio Settings**, set **Suppress background noise** to *Auto* or *Low* for most situations.  
- **Original Sound** – If you need high‑fidelity audio (e.g., playing a music demo), enable **Show “Original Sound”** and toggle it on during the meeting.

---

## 3. Engaging Participants: Chat, Reactions, and Raised Hand  

Interaction keeps meetings dynamic and helps you gauge understanding.

### 3.1 Using the Chat Pane  

1. Click **Chat** on the toolbar.  
2. By default, the pane opens on the right side.  
3. **Select recipients** from the drop‑down menu:  
   * **All Participants** – broadcast to everyone.  
   * **Specific participant** – private message.  
4. Type your message and press **Enter**.  
5. Participants can reply in the same pane; the conversation scrolls automatically.

> **Best practice:** Encourage participants to use the chat for **questions** or **links** they want to share, rather than lengthy discussions that belong in the main conversation.

### 3.2 Reactions (Emoji)  

Zoom offers quick, non‑verbal feedback:

- Hover near the bottom‑left of the screen; a small **emoji** icon appears.  
- Click **Raise Hand**, **Thumbs Up**, **Clap**, **Smile**, or **Love**.  
- The reaction appears briefly on the participant’s video tile and in the participant list.

### 3.3 The Raised‑Hand Feature  

When a participant clicks **Raise Hand**, their hand icon appears next to their name in the Participants panel. As host, you can:

1. **Acknowledge** them by calling on them verbally.  
2. **Spotlight** their video if they need to present.  
3. **Lower** the hand (click the hand icon next to their name) once they’ve spoken.

> **Tip:** Use the **Raise Hand** queue to manage Q&A sessions, especially when you have many attendees.

---

## 4. Sharing Content  

Whether you need to display a slide deck, demonstrate an app, or brainstorm on a virtual whiteboard, Zoom’s **Share Screen** feature covers all three.

### 4.1 Sharing Your Entire Desktop vs. Specific Windows  

1. Click **Share Screen** on the toolbar.  
2. A dialog shows all available options:  
   * **Desktop** – shares everything you see on your monitor.  
   * **Window** – lists open applications (e.g., PowerPoint, Chrome). Choose the one you want to share.  
3. **Check** the **Share computer sound** box if you’ll be playing audio (e.g., a video clip).  
4. Click **Share**.

> **When to use each:**  
> * **Desktop** – useful for multitasking or when you’ll switch between several apps.  
> * **Window** – more privacy‑friendly; only the selected app is visible to others.

### 4.2 Sharing a Specific Application  

If you’re demoing a software tool:

1. Open the application **before** you click **Share Screen** (helps it appear in the window list).  
2. In the share dialog, select the application’s window.  
3. Click **Share**.  
4. The participants will see only that app, even if you move to another program on your screen.

### 4.3 Using the Built‑In Whiteboard  

Zoom includes a simple whiteboard for quick sketches:

1. In the **Share Screen** dialog, select **Whiteboard** (usually at the top).  
2. Click **Share**.  
3. A toolbar appears with drawing tools: **Pen**, **Highlighter**, **Eraser**, **Stamp**, and **Text**.  
4. Draw, annotate, or write as needed.  
5. Participants can be granted **annotation rights** by clicking **More** → **Allow participants to annotate**.

> **Scenario:** During the pitch, you can draw a quick diagram to illustrate a workflow, then save the whiteboard as an image (click **More** → **Save**).

### 4.4 Managing Shared Content  

- **Pause Share** – Click **Pause Share** on the toolbar if you need a brief interruption without stopping the session.  
- **Stop Share** – When you’re done, click **Stop Share** (or press **Esc**).  
- **Switch Sources** – Click **Share Screen** again to switch to a different window or the whiteboard without leaving the meeting.

---

## 5. Quick‑Reference Checklist for a Smooth Live Meeting  

| Step | Action | Where |
|------|--------|-------|
| 1 | Verify microphone & camera on pre‑join screen | All devices |
| 2 | Start/join meeting (client, web, mobile) | **Zoom Client**, `zoom.us/join`, mobile app |
| 3 | Mute yourself; mute all participants if needed | Toolbar → Participants panel |
| 4 | Spotlight speaker (optional) | Participants → More → Spotlight Video |
| 5 | Enable chat, reactions, raise‑hand | Toolbar (Chat, Reactions) |
| 6 | Share screen (desktop, window, or whiteboard) | Toolbar → Share Screen |
| 7 | Use **Pause Share** for brief breaks | Toolbar while sharing |
| 8 | End meeting (host) | Toolbar → End Meeting → End Meeting for All |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Start a meeting** from any device—desktop client, web browser, or mobile app—by entering the Meeting ID or clicking the scheduled link.  
- **Audio/video controls** are available on the toolbar; as host you can mute all, allow unmuting, and spotlight a participant’s video.  
- **Participant interaction** is facilitated through the chat pane, emoji reactions, and the raised‑hand feature, which help manage questions and feedback.  
- **Sharing content** works via **Share Screen**: choose the whole desktop, a specific application window, or Zoom’s built‑in whiteboard; remember to enable “Share computer sound” for videos.  
- A short **checklist** before and during the meeting ensures you cover all essential steps, keeping the session professional and focused.

modules.title: Collaboration Features: Breakout Rooms, Polls, and Whiteboard
modules.content:
## Turning One‑to‑Many Sessions into Small‑Group Workshops  

Imagine you are leading a product‑launch meeting with 30 regional sales managers. After a brief presentation, you need each team to brainstorm pricing ideas **in parallel** and then report back to the whole group. Doing this in a single Zoom window would be chaotic—people would talk over each other, and you’d lose track of who contributed what.  

Zoom’s **breakout rooms**, **polls**, and **whiteboard** tools let you split the large audience into focused groups, capture their input instantly, and bring the results back to the main session—all without leaving the meeting. The following sections walk you through setting up each tool, using it live, and preserving the outcomes for later review.

---

## Setting Up Breakout Rooms  

Breakout rooms are separate “mini‑meetings” that run inside your main Zoom session. Participants can be placed **manually** (you choose who goes where) or **automatically** (Zoom distributes them evenly).  

### 1. Enable Breakout Rooms in Your Account (once‑off step)  

> *If you have already scheduled a meeting, you can still enable breakout rooms from the meeting controls; however, enabling it at the account level ensures the option appears for every host you designate.*  

1. Sign in to the Zoom web portal (open a web browser and go to zoom.us).  
2. Click **Settings** in the left‑hand menu.  
3. Under the **In Meeting (Advanced)** tab, locate **Breakout room** and toggle it **On**.  
4. (Optional) Check **Allow host to assign participants to breakout rooms manually** if you prefer manual assignment.  

> **Tip:** The setting may be disabled by your organization’s administrator. If you see a lock icon, contact your IT admin.

### 2. Create Breakout Rooms During a Live Meeting  

1. In the meeting window, click **Breakout Rooms** on the toolbar (you’ll find it next to **Chat** and **Reactions**).  
2. A dialog appears asking **How many rooms** you need and **Assign participants**:  
   * **Manually** – you will drag and drop names.  
   * **Automatically** – Zoom distributes participants evenly.  
3. Choose the number of rooms (e.g., 3) and the assignment method.  

#### Manual Assignment Workflow  

* After clicking **Create**, a list of participant names appears on the left.  
* Drag each name into the desired room on the right, or click **Assign** next to a name and select the target room from a dropdown.  

#### Automatic Assignment Workflow  

* Select **Automatically** and click **Create**.  
* Zoom instantly splits participants into the specified number of rooms, balancing the count as evenly as possible.  

4. (Optional) Click **Options** to set:  
   * **Allow participants to return to the main session** – lets attendees leave the room on their own.  
   * **Open rooms automatically** – rooms open as soon as they’re created; otherwise, you’ll open them manually.  

5. Click **Open All Rooms** when you’re ready to start the small‑group work. Participants receive a prompt to join their assigned room.

### 3. Managing Breakout Rooms While They’re Active  

* **Broadcast a message** – Click **Broadcast a message to all** to send the same text to every room (e.g., “You have 10 minutes left”).  
* **Move participants** – If you need to rebalance groups, click **Move** next to a participant’s name and select a new room.  
* **Close rooms** – When the activity ends, click **Close All Rooms**. Attendees see a countdown (default 60 seconds) before being returned to the main session.  

### 4. Saving Breakout Room Data  

Zoom does not automatically record each breakout room’s audio/video, but you can **record** them individually if you enable the feature beforehand:

1. Before the meeting, go to **Settings → Recording** on the web portal.  
2. Turn **Local Recording** (or **Cloud Recording**) **On**.  
3. In the meeting, click **More** → **Record on this Computer** (or **Record to the Cloud**) **before** opening breakout rooms.  
4. Each breakout room will generate a separate file, labeled with the room number.  

If you only need the **list of participants per room**, click **Export** in the Breakout Rooms dialog after the session ends. The CSV file contains participant names and the room they were assigned to.

---

## Running Live Polls to Capture Immediate Feedback  

Polls are quick, multiple‑choice questions that appear in the meeting window. They’re ideal for gauging understanding, prioritizing ideas, or taking a quick vote.  

### 1. Prepare Your Polls Ahead of Time  

1. Open the Zoom web portal and navigate to **Meetings → Upcoming**.  
2. Click the meeting you’ll host, then select **Poll** in the menu.  
3. Click **Add** to create a new poll.  
   * **Title** – e.g., “Pricing Strategy Preference”.  
   * **Question** – type the prompt.  
   * **Answer type** – choose **Single choice** (one answer) or **Multiple choice** (allow more than one).  
   * **Answers** – enter each option on a separate line.  
4. Click **Save**. You can add multiple polls to the same meeting; they will appear in the order you create them.  

> **Pro tip:** Keep each poll to **no more than 5‑7 options**; longer lists can overwhelm participants and slow down response times.

### 2. Launch a Poll During the Meeting  

1. In the meeting toolbar, click **Polls**.  
2. Select the poll you want to launch from the dropdown list.  
3. Click **Launch Poll**. Participants see the question instantly.  

#### Monitoring Results  

* While the poll is live, you can view a **real‑time bar chart** showing how many people selected each answer.  
* Click **End Poll** when you’re ready to stop collecting responses.  

#### Sharing Results  

* After ending the poll, you’ll see a **Results** screen.  
* Click **Share** to display the results to all participants.  
* Optionally, click **Download** to save the results as a **CSV file** for later analysis.  

### 3. Using Polls for Group Decision‑Making  

During a breakout‑room activity, you might want each group to vote on its best idea. Here’s a quick workflow:

1. **Create a poll** with the options representing each group’s suggestion (e.g., “Group A – Discount 10%”, “Group B – Bundle Offer”).  
2. **Assign participants** to breakout rooms and let them discuss.  
3. **Return to the main session**, launch the poll, and let the entire audience vote.  
4. **Share the results** instantly, then discuss the winning idea.  

---

## Whiteboard and Annotation: Visual Brainstorming in Real Time  

The **whiteboard** is a blank canvas that any participant can draw on, type on, or add sticky‑note‑like annotations. It works whether you’re in the main session or a breakout room.  

### 1. Opening the Whiteboard  

1. Click **Share Screen** on the meeting toolbar.  
2. In the sharing options, select **Whiteboard** (you’ll see a thumbnail labeled “Whiteboard”).  
3. Click **Share**.  

> **Note:** If you have multiple monitors, you can choose which screen to share, but the whiteboard option works independently of your desktop view.

### 2. Core Annotation Tools  

At the top of the whiteboard, a toolbar provides:

| Icon | Name | Quick Use |
|------|------|-----------|
| ✏️ | **Pen** | Freehand drawing. Choose color and thickness. |
| 📐 | **Line** | Straight lines; hold **Shift** for perfect horizontal/vertical lines. |
| ⬜ | **Rectangle / Circle** | Click‑drag to create shapes. |
| 🖍️ | **Highlighter** | Semi‑transparent color for emphasizing text. |
| 📍 | **Text** | Click anywhere to type. Font size can be adjusted via the dropdown. |
| 📎 | **Stamp** | Pre‑made symbols (checkmark, X, arrow). |
| 🗑️ | **Eraser** | Remove unwanted strokes; toggle **Erase All** to clear the board. |
| 📎 | **Spotlight** (host only) | Highlight a specific participant’s cursor for everyone to follow. |

### 3. Collaboration Flow  

1. **Introduce the canvas** – “We’ll use the whiteboard to map out our pricing ideas.”  
2. **Assign roles** – In a breakout room, ask one person to sketch while another types notes.  
3. **Use the **Spotlight** tool** – As the host, click **Spotlight** on a participant’s cursor to draw attention to their contribution.  
4. **Encourage annotation** – Participants can add sticky‑note‑style text boxes by selecting **Text** and typing short ideas.  

### 4. Saving and Exporting the Whiteboard  

When the session ends (or whenever you’re ready):

1. Click **More** (three dots) in the whiteboard toolbar.  
2. Choose **Save**. Zoom prompts you to select a location on your computer (or, if you’re using Cloud Recording, the whiteboard is saved automatically with the recording).  
3. The file saves as a **PNG image**.  

If you have multiple whiteboards (e.g., one per breakout room), repeat the save step for each. You can then **insert** these images into meeting minutes, PowerPoint decks, or share them via email.

> **Alternative:** If you’re recording the meeting to the Cloud, the whiteboard appears as a separate **recorded file** that can be downloaded later.

---

## Integrating the Three Tools in a Single Session  

Below is a concise, step‑by‑step script you can follow for a typical collaborative meeting:

| Phase | Action | Zoom Feature |
|-------|--------|--------------|
| **Opening** | Brief presentation of objectives | Standard screen share |
| **Group Work** | Split attendees into 4 breakout rooms | **Breakout Rooms – Automatic** |
| **Brainstorm** | Teams use whiteboard to sketch ideas | **Whiteboard** inside each breakout |
| **Regroup** | Return to main session; each team presents | **Close Breakout Rooms** |
| **Vote** | Whole group votes on the best idea | **Poll** (single‑choice) |
| **Wrap‑up** | Share poll results, save whiteboards | **Export Poll CSV** + **Save Whiteboard PNG** |

By following this flow, you keep the meeting **structured**, **interactive**, and **recorded** for future reference.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Hurdles  

| Issue | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|-------|--------------|-----------|
| Participants can’t see the whiteboard | Host didn’t share the whiteboard screen | Click **Share Screen → Whiteboard** again |
| Poll button is missing | Polls not enabled in account settings | Enable **Polling** under **Settings → In Meeting (Advanced)** |
| Breakout rooms close unexpectedly | Host clicked **Close All Rooms** by accident | Re‑open rooms via **Breakout Rooms → Open All Rooms** (participants will be prompted to re‑join) |
| Whiteboard annotations disappear after saving | Saved before finishing drawing | Ensure you click **Save** **after** all participants are done; otherwise, ask them to finish then save again |

---

## Best Practices for a Smooth Collaborative Experience  

* **Pre‑plan your rooms** – Know how many groups you need and whether you’ll assign manually (useful for specific expertise) or automatically (faster).  
* **Test polls** – Run a quick “test poll” with a simple yes/no question to confirm participants can see and answer.  
* **Limit whiteboard clutter** – Encourage concise notes; too many scribbles can make the final image hard to read.  
* **Designate a “room facilitator”** – In each breakout room, assign one person to keep the group on task and to summarize the outcome on the whiteboard.  
* **Export everything** – After the meeting, download the poll CSV and whiteboard PNGs, then store them in a shared folder (e.g., your company’s SharePoint or Google Drive) for easy access by all participants.  

---

## Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: Can participants launch polls themselves?**  
A: Only the host (or co‑host) can create and launch polls during a meeting. However, you can give a trusted participant co‑host rights under **Participants → More → Make Co‑Host**.

**Q: Are breakout rooms available on mobile devices?**  
A: Yes. Participants see a **Join** button when a room opens. Hosts on mobile can create rooms via the **More** menu, though the full manual assignment UI is easier on desktop.

**Q: Do whiteboard annotations persist after the meeting ends if I’m not recording?**  
A: Yes, as long as the host clicks **Save** before closing the meeting. The saved PNG captures the final state of the board.

**Q: How many participants can join a single whiteboard?**  
A: All participants in the meeting (or breakout room) can annotate simultaneously. Performance may degrade with very large numbers (e.g., >100), so consider splitting into smaller groups if needed.

---

## Quick Reference Checklist  

- **Enable** Breakout Rooms, Polls, and Whiteboard in your account settings.  
- **Create** breakout rooms → **Manual** or **Automatic** assignment.  
- **Launch** the Whiteboard → **Share Screen → Whiteboard**.  
- **Add** Polls in the web portal → **Launch** from meeting toolbar.  
- **Save** Whiteboard (PNG) and **Export** Poll results (CSV) after the meeting.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- Breakout rooms let you divide a large meeting into focused small groups, with both manual and automatic assignment options.  
- Live polls provide instant, quantifiable feedback; they can be prepared ahead of time and the results exported as CSV files.  
- The whiteboard and its annotation tools support visual brainstorming; saved images capture the collaborative output for later use.  
- By combining breakout rooms, polls, and whiteboard in a single session, you can run structured, interactive workshops that keep participants engaged and produce tangible deliverables.

modules.title: Security and Privacy Best Practices
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call  

Imagine you’re about to host a quarterly review with a new client. The agenda is set, the slides are polished, and the Zoom link has been emailed to the participants. Five minutes before the start, a stranger pops into the meeting, sees confidential financial data on your screen, and asks a question that makes no sense. The meeting is interrupted, the client’s trust is shaken, and you scramble to remove the intruder.  

This scenario is all too common. The good news is that with a few simple settings—waiting rooms, passwords, permission controls, role assignments, and encryption—you can lock the virtual door before the first participant joins. The steps below walk you through each of these safeguards, assuming you’ve already learned how to schedule meetings and start a live session in earlier chapters.

---

## 1. The Baseline: Why Security and Privacy Matter  

* **Confidentiality:** Business conversations often contain trade secrets, financial figures, or personal data. Unauthorized eyes can lead to legal or reputational damage.  
* **Trust:** Clients and employees expect a safe environment. Demonstrating proactive security builds confidence.  
* **Compliance:** Regulations such as GDPR, HIPAA, or industry‑specific policies may require encryption and strict access controls.  

Even if you’re only meeting with internal teammates, the same principles apply. Treat every Zoom meeting like a physical conference room: you lock the door, check who’s inside, and control who can move objects around.

---

## 2. Locking the Door – Enabling Waiting Rooms and Meeting Passwords  

### 2.1 What Is a Waiting Room?  

A **waiting room** is a virtual lobby where participants sit until you admit them. It acts like a receptionist, letting you verify each attendee before they join the main session.

### 2.2 Turn On the Waiting Room (Global Setting)  

1. Open the Zoom web portal (zoom.us) and sign in.  
2. Navigate to **Settings** → **Security**.  
3. Locate **Waiting Room** and toggle it **On**.  

> **Tip:** Enabling it globally means every new meeting you create will have the waiting room feature automatically available. You can still disable it for a specific meeting if needed.

### 2.3 Enable Waiting Room for a Single Meeting  

When you schedule a meeting (see *Scheduling and Managing Meetings*), scroll to the **Meeting Options** section:

1. Check **Enable waiting room**.  
2. Click **Save**.

During a live session (see *Running a Live Meeting*), you can also turn it on from the **Security** button on the meeting toolbar.

### 2.4 What Is a Meeting Password?  

A **meeting password** is a short string (usually 6‑10 characters) that participants must enter after clicking the meeting link. It adds a second layer of protection, especially when the link is shared publicly.

### 2.5 Set a Password When Scheduling  

1. In the **Schedule a Meeting** screen, find the **Password** field.  
2. Click **Generate** for a random password or type your own.  
3. Click **Save**.

### 2.6 Best Practices for Passwords  

- **Use a unique password** for each meeting; avoid reusing the same string.  
- **Share the password securely** (e.g., via encrypted email, a password‑protected document, or a corporate chat tool).  
- **Avoid obvious patterns** like “123456” or “meeting2024”.  

### 2.7 Putting It Together: A Quick Walkthrough  

1. **Schedule** the meeting → enable **Waiting Room** and **Password**.  
2. **Distribute** the link **and** password through a secure channel.  
3. **Start** the meeting → admit participants from the waiting room after confirming their identity.  

With these steps, only invited people can enter, and you retain control over who joins.

---

## 3. Controlling Participant Permissions  

Once participants are inside, you decide what they can do. Zoom groups several actions under **Participant Permissions**, which you can set globally (in Settings) or per meeting.

### 3.1 Key Permission Types  

| Permission | What It Controls | Typical Use |
|------------|------------------|-------------|
| **Screen Sharing** | Who can share their screen or a specific application | Allow only the host for confidential presentations; enable for all when collaboration is needed |
| **Annotation** | Ability to draw on shared content | Useful for brainstorming; disable to prevent accidental markings |
| **Chat** | Public chat, private chat, and file sharing | Restrict to host‑only chat for Q&A sessions |
| **Rename** | Whether participants can change their displayed name | Enforce real names for accountability |
| **Polling** | Ability to launch polls | Enable if you plan to gather instant feedback |

### 3.2 Setting Default Permissions (Global)  

1. In the web portal, go to **Settings** → **In Meeting (Basic)**.  
2. Find each permission toggle (e.g., **Share Screen**, **Annotation**) and set the default you prefer.  

### 3.3 Adjusting Permissions for a Specific Meeting  

During the live meeting, click the **Security** button on the toolbar. You’ll see a list of checkboxes:

- **Allow participants to share screen**  
- **Allow annotation**  
- **Allow chat** (Public/Private)  

Check or uncheck each option based on the meeting’s purpose.

### 3.4 Scenario: Preventing an Accidental Screen Share  

You’re presenting a confidential product roadmap. You want only the host to share screens:

1. **Before the meeting**, set the global default: **Only host can share screen**.  
2. **During the meeting**, keep the waiting room enabled. Admit participants only after confirming their identity.  
3. If a participant tries to share, Zoom will prompt them with a “Host only” notice, preventing any accidental exposure.

---

## 4. Host vs. Co‑Host – Roles and How to Assign Them  

### 4.1 Definitions  

- **Host:** The person who created the meeting or was assigned the host role. The host has full control over all settings, participants, and recordings.  
- **Co‑host:** A participant granted many of the host’s privileges (e.g., admit from waiting room, mute participants, manage breakout rooms) without being the primary host.  

### 4.2 When to Use a Co‑Host  

- **Large meetings** where the host needs assistance managing participants.  
- **Webinars** or training sessions where a presenter focuses on content while a co‑host handles technical issues.  
- **Recurring team meetings** where ownership rotates among members.

### 4.3 Enabling the Co‑Host Feature  

1. In the web portal, navigate to **Settings** → **In Meeting (Advanced)**.  
2. Toggle **Co‑host** to **On**.  

> **Note:** The co‑host option must be enabled before you can assign anyone the role.

### 4.4 Assigning a Co‑Host During a Live Meeting  

1. Open the **Participants** panel.  
2. Hover over the participant’s name, click **More**, then select **Make Co‑Host**.  
3. The participant’s name will now display a co‑host badge, and they’ll receive a notification of their new rights.

### 4.5 Pre‑Assigning Co‑Hosts When Scheduling  

If you know who should share host duties ahead of time:

1. In the **Schedule a Meeting** screen, scroll to **Meeting Options**.  
2. Click **Alternative Hosts** and type the email addresses of the users you want to give co‑host rights.  
3. Save the meeting.  

When the meeting starts, those users will automatically have co‑host privileges.

### 4.6 Best Practices for Role Management  

- **Limit co‑hosts** to trusted team members.  
- **Document** who holds co‑host rights for each recurring meeting.  
- **Revoke** co‑host status promptly after the meeting ends (Zoom does this automatically, but double‑check for ongoing sessions).

---

## 5. Encryption – Protecting Data In‑Transit and At‑Rest  

### 5.1 What Is Encryption?  

**Encryption** scrambles data so that only authorized parties can read it. In Zoom, there are two primary layers:

1. **Transport Encryption (TLS):** Secures the data as it travels between your device and Zoom’s servers. This is enabled by default for all meetings.  
2. **End‑to‑End Encryption (E2EE):** Scrambles the data on the sender’s device and only the receiver’s device can decrypt it—Zoom’s servers never see the unencrypted content.

### 5.2 When to Use End‑to‑End Encryption  

- **Highly confidential meetings** (e.g., legal counsel, medical consultations).  
- **Regulatory environments** that require the strongest possible protection.  

### 5.3 Enabling E2EE  

1. Go to **Settings** → **Security** on the web portal.  
2. Find **End‑to‑End Encryption** and toggle it **On**.  
3. When scheduling a meeting, you’ll see a new option: **Enable End‑to‑End Encryption**. Check it.  

> **Limitations:** With E2EE turned on, certain features are disabled, such as cloud recording, live transcription, and joining by phone. Review the warning message before enabling it.

### 5.4 Verifying Encryption Status During a Meeting  

- Click the **i** (information) icon on the meeting toolbar.  
- Look for **“Encryption: End‑to‑End”** under the meeting details.  

If you see **“Encryption: Transport”**, the meeting is using TLS but not E2EE.

### 5.5 Quick Checklist for Encryption  

| Feature | TLS (Default) | End‑to‑End Encryption |
|---------|----------------|------------------------|
| Cloud recording | ✅ | ❌ |
| Phone dial‑in | ✅ | ❌ |
| Live transcription | ✅ | ❌ |
| Highest privacy level | — | ✅ |

Choose the level that matches your meeting’s sensitivity.

---

## 6. Staying Current – Security Updates and Ongoing Best Practices  

### 6.1 Why Updates Matter  

Zoom releases frequent patches that address newly discovered vulnerabilities, improve encryption, and add security features. Running an outdated client can expose you to risks that have already been fixed.

### 6.2 How to Keep Your Zoom Client Fresh  

| Platform | How to Update |
|----------|---------------|
| **Desktop (Windows/macOS)** | Open the Zoom client → click your profile picture → **Check for Updates**. |
| **Mobile (iOS/Android)** | Visit the **App Store** or **Google Play Store**, locate **Zoom Cloud Meetings**, and tap **Update**. |
| **Web Browser** | No client needed; just ensure your browser is up to date. |

Enable automatic updates if your organization’s policy allows it.

### 6.3 Monitoring Zoom’s Security Blog  

Zoom maintains a **Security Blog** that announces major changes, new compliance certifications, and best‑practice guides. Bookmark https://zoom.us/security and review it monthly.

### 6.4 Ongoing Security Checklist  

- **Before each meeting:**  
  1. Verify waiting room is active.  
  2. Confirm a password is set (or use a unique meeting ID).  
  3. Review participant permissions.  
  4. Ensure the correct host/co‑host roles are assigned.  
  5. Check encryption status (especially for confidential sessions).  

- **After each meeting:**  
  1. End the meeting and **Lock** it (optional, prevents late joiners).  
  2. Review the participant list for any unexpected names.  
  3. Log out of the Zoom client if you’re on a shared device.  

- **Monthly:**  
  1. Install any pending client updates.  
  2. Re‑evaluate global security settings (waiting room, co‑host, E2EE).  
  3. Scan the Zoom Security Blog for new recommendations.  

### 6.5 Real‑World Reminder  

A mid‑size tech firm once postponed a software demo because an employee accidentally left the meeting unlocked after the presentation ended. A stray participant joined, asked a few unrelated questions, and then left. The incident prompted the team to adopt a **post‑meeting lock** habit and to double‑check the waiting room setting before every session. Small procedural tweaks can prevent embarrassing or risky moments.

---

## 7. One‑Click Security Checklist  

| ✅ | Action |
|----|--------|
| 1️⃣ | **Enable Waiting Room** (global or per‑meeting) |
| 2️⃣ | **Set a Unique Password** for every meeting |
| 3️⃣ | **Control Permissions** – screen sharing, annotation, chat |
| 4️⃣ | **Assign Co‑hosts** where needed |
| 5️⃣ | **Turn on End‑to‑End Encryption** for confidential calls |
| 6️⃣ | **Check for Client Updates** before each session |
| 7️⃣ | **Lock the Meeting** after all intended participants have joined (optional) |
| 8️⃣ | **Review Participant List** after the meeting ends |

Print this checklist and keep it handy on your desk or as a digital note. A quick glance before you click “Start” can save you from a security breach later.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Waiting rooms and passwords** act as the first line of defense; always enable them.  
- **Participant permissions** let you tailor what attendees can do, protecting shared content and preventing disruptions.  
- **Host and co‑host roles** distribute control responsibly; pre‑assign co‑hosts for larger or recurring meetings.  
- **End‑to‑End Encryption** offers the strongest privacy, but be aware of feature trade‑offs.  
- **Stay updated** by regularly installing Zoom client updates and reviewing the Zoom Security Blog.  
- Use the **one‑click security checklist** before every meeting to ensure no step is missed.  

By consistently applying these practices, you’ll create a secure Zoom environment that safeguards your business information, respects participant privacy, and projects professionalism to every attendee.

modules.title: Recording, Storing, and Sharing Meeting Content
modules.content:
## Capture the Moment: Why Recording Matters  

Imagine you’ve just wrapped up a 45‑minute product demo for a prospective client. The meeting ran smoothly, the client asked several insightful questions, and the sales lead promised to follow up. A week later, the client asks for a copy of the presentation to share with their technical team. If you hadn’t recorded the session, you’d have to recreate the slides from memory—or risk losing the momentum entirely.  

Recording meetings in Zoom gives you a reliable “golden copy” of what was said, shown, and decided. Whether you need a reference for internal training, a compliance audit, or a simple share‑back with participants, the ability to record, store, and distribute content is a core business skill that every Zoom beginner should master.

---

## 1. Choose the Right Recording Mode  

Zoom offers two distinct recording destinations:

| **Recording Type** | **Where It Is Saved** | **When to Use It** |
|--------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|
| **Local Recording** | On the computer that hosts the meeting (hard drive) | Small teams, limited cloud storage, or when you need an immediate file without internet latency |
| **Cloud Recording** | In Zoom’s secure online storage (accessible via the Zoom web portal) | Larger organizations, need for automatic transcripts, or when you want to share a link without sending large files |

### 1.1 Enable Recording Permissions  

Before you can start any recording, you must have the appropriate permission:

1. **Host Permission** – By default, only the meeting host can record.  
2. **Participant Permission** – If you want a co‑host or another participant to record, go to **Settings → Recording** in the Zoom web portal and toggle **“Allow participants to record”**.  

> **Tip:** For ad‑hoc meetings, you can also grant “record” rights on the fly. In the meeting controls, click **Participants**, hover over a participant’s name, click **More**, then select **Allow Record**.

### 1.2 Selecting Local vs. Cloud Recording  

1. **Open the Zoom client** (refer to *Running a Live Meeting* for basic navigation).  
2. Click the **Record** button in the control bar.  
   - If you see **“Record on this Computer”**, you’re set for a local recording.  
   - If you see **“Record to the Cloud”**, your account has cloud recording enabled.  

> **Note:** Some free accounts only support local recording, while paid plans unlock cloud recording and additional storage.

---

## 2. Start Recording and Pick a Layout  

### 2.1 Starting the Recording  

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Click **Record** (or **Record on this Computer** / **Record to the Cloud**) in the meeting toolbar. |
| 2 | A small **Recording** indicator appears in the top‑left corner, confirming that Zoom is capturing the session. |
| 3 | To pause, click **Pause**; to resume, click **Resume**. Use **Stop Recording** when the meeting ends. |

> **Pro tip:** Pause recording during unrelated chit‑chat (e.g., “water‑cooler” talk) to keep the final file concise.

### 2.2 Choosing a Recording Layout  

Zoom lets you decide how the video is composed:

1. **Active Speaker** – Shows the person currently speaking.  
2. **Gallery View** – Displays up to 49 participants in a grid (cloud recordings only).  
3. **Shared Screen Only** – Captures only the screen share, omitting participant video.  

**How to set the layout before recording starts:**

- **Local Recording:** Click the **arrow** next to the **Record** button → **Recording Settings** → **Layout**. Choose **Active Speaker**, **Gallery View**, or **Share Screen Only**.  
- **Cloud Recording:** In the Zoom web portal, go to **Settings → Recording → Cloud Recording** and toggle the desired layout options (e.g., “Record active speaker with shared screen”).  

> **Scenario:** A training session where the presenter’s slides are the focus should use **Shared Screen Only** to keep the file size small and the visual emphasis clear.

---

## 3. Locate and Manage Your Recordings  

### 3.1 Accessing Local Recordings  

1. After the meeting ends, Zoom automatically processes the file.  
2. A dialog box appears showing the folder location (by default: **Documents → Zoom → [Meeting ID]**).  
3. Inside you’ll find separate files for video (**.mp4**), audio (**.m4a**), and chat transcript (**.txt**).  

**Changing the default folder:**  
- Open **Zoom → Settings → Recording** and click **Change** next to **Store my recordings at**.
